extracted.intended_audience: authors, typists, and copy editors typesetting mathematical documents with TeX (mathematicians and technical writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and conventions for entering and formatting mathematical formulas in (plain) TeX: character meanings in math mode, accenting, fractions and styles, delimiters, and spacing/positioning controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform positioning of overlines and roots with \mathstrut
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \mathstrut to force subformulas to have the same height and depth so that constructs like square roots and overlines align uniformly across terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A \mathstrut is an invisible box with zero width whose height and depth equal those of a parenthesis 'T'. Example: $\sqrt{\mathstrut a}+\sqrt{\mathstrut d}+\sqrt{\mathstrut y}$. For more complete control of positioning use \smash and \phantom (discussed in Chapter 18).

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX knows box dimensions of letters/subformulas
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX treats every letter and subformula as a box and therefore knows its height, depth, and width for positioning accents, bars, roots, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underlies automatic placement of constructs like \overline, \underline, and \sqrt; when you want uniformity across different members of a complex formula you may need explicit boxes (e.g., \mathstrut).

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters are 'ordinary symbols' (variables) in math mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The 52 letters A–Z and a–z denote italic symbols (variables) and are treated as ordinary symbols in math mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are font/variant considerations (e.g., alternative glyphs for certain lowercase letters). Traditionally use the italic letter unless a different form (like \ell) is specifically requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain characters remain roman and act as ordinary symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Digits 0–9 and a set of punctuation characters (! ? | : etc.) are treated as ordinary symbols and remain in roman type when used in formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to distinguish letter O and numeral 0, and watch for placement before left parentheses (e.g., use x_O rather than x_0 in some contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary operations (+, -, *) spacing/behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters +, -, and * are treated as binary operations (they operate on two parts of a formula) and receive spacing appropriate for binary operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate how TeX spaces them. Note - and * produce different glyph shapes in math mode. Binary operators behave as ordinary symbols if not placed between two operable quantities (e.g., in 'x=+1' or in superscripts/subscripts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Slash '/' treated as ordinary symbol (not binary operation)
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX does not treat '/' as a binary operation; it is treated as an ordinary symbol to preserve traditional spacing around slashes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids incorrect extra space in constructs like $1/2$. Use grouping/braces to control how \over applies relative to slashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations (=, <, >, :) are a distinct class with specific spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters =, <, >, and : are treated as relations and receive different spacing than binary operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many other relation symbols are available via control sequences (see Appendix F). Use appropriate relation symbols (\le, \ne, \sim, \equiv, \subset, etc.) as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma and semicolon are punctuation in math mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma (,) and semicolon (;) are treated as punctuation marks in formulas: TeX inserts a little extra space after them but not before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f(x,y;z). If you need a comma to act as an ordinary symbol (e.g., in large numbers) put it in braces: 12{,}345x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period is ordinary symbol; colon can be punctuation via \colon
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is treated as an ordinary symbol (no extra space after it in formulas); use \colon to make ':' behave as punctuation instead of a relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f:A\to B versus f\colon A\to B (the latter has spacing like a punctuation mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Openings and closings help TeX detect binary usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses, brackets, braces and similar opening/closing characters act mostly like ordinary symbols but inform TeX when something is not a binary operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of how delimiters affect spacing rules; use \lbrace/\rbrace for braces since { and } are grouping characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved characters and grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX reserves ten characters (\, $, %, #, &, ~, {, }, ^, _) that cannot be used as ordinary math symbols unless their catcodes are changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use { } for grouping; use control sequences (e.g., \lbrace, \rbrace) to get literal braces. Avoid changing conventions except for special needs (see Chapter 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ^ and _ only in math mode (alternatives \sp and \sb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Superscript (^) and subscript (_) characters should be used only inside math mode; if unavailable you can use \sp and \sb instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: $x\sp2$ is equivalent to $x^2$. TeX uses the presence of math-only constructs to detect missing $ characters in the source and will attempt to recover from some mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX recovers from missing $ via math-only tokens; blank lines not allowed in math mode
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX can detect some missing dollar-sign mistakes when math-only tokens appear, and will insert $ automatically or give an error; a blank line (\par) is not permitted in math mode and also provides a recovery mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example error scenario: The smallest $n such that $2^n>1000$ is~10. TeX will attempt to resynchronize and confine errors to the paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math accents: dedicated accent commands and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides math accents (\hat, \check, \tilde, \acute, \grave, \dot, \ddot, \breve, \bar, \vee) which are distinct from text accents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TeX will complain if you try to use text accent commands in math mode or math accents in text. Define control sequences (macros) for frequently used accented letters to save keystrokes (examples: \def\Ahat{{\hat A}}). Use \imath and \jmath (dotless i/j) when placing accents over i or j.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stacked accents and \skew for superaccents
rubrics_metrics.description: You can place accents on top of accents (superaccents) but must adjust horizontal placement; plain TeX provides \skew<n> to shift superaccents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the skew amount by trial and error (example: \skew6\hat\Ahat). The exact value depends on font metrics and visual preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between \bar and \overline; \widehat/\widetilde available
rubrics_metrics.description: \bar is a fixed-length accent while \overline grows with the width of the underlying formula; \widehat and \widetilde are growing accents for wider arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may prefer \overline for a longer line even on a single letter. Examples: $\bar z + \overline z$. Also show \widehat{xy}, \widetilde{xyz} to illustrate growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: \over applies to entire (braced) subformula; avoid multiple \over in same subformula
rubrics_metrics.description: The control sequence \over applies to everything in the current (or braced) subformula; you cannot use \over twice in the same subformula without grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of 'a \over b \over 2' use either '{a\over b}\over2' or 'a\over{b\over2}', though both can look awkward. Editors should convert complex built-up fractions to slashed form (a/b) or appropriate regrouping for clarity and readability. Use parentheses around fraction parts when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer slashed form for awkward built-up fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: When built-up \over constructions become too small or crowded, convert to slashed form (a/b) and add parentheses as needed to preserve meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a/b over 2' or 'a over b/2' are preferable to nested \over constructs. Conversion to slashed form requires mathematical judgement about where to put parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special fraction-like operations: \atop, \choose, \above
rubrics_metrics.description: \atop behaves like \over but omits the fraction line; \choose encloses result in parentheses (commonly used for binomial coefficients); \above{dimen} lets you specify the rule thickness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot mix \over, \atop, and \choose without grouping. Examples: $$n\choose k$$ and using \above to make a heavier main bar (e.g., \above1pt).

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX's styles and size rules (D, D', T, T', S, S', SS, SS')
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX has eight math styles (display/text/script/scriptscript and cramped variants). These styles determine type size (text size, script size, scriptscript size) and the sizing/positioning of subscripts, superscripts, numerators, and denominators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display formulas (enclosed in $$...$$) are in display style (D), inline $...$ are text style (T). Subformula style transitions are defined (e.g., numerator/denominator styles when using \over depend on parent style). There is no scriptscriptscript size beyond SS; smallest is scriptscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Override automatic style selection with \displaystyle, \textstyle, \scriptstyle, \scriptscriptstyle
rubrics_metrics.description: You can explicitly select the style you want for a formula or subformula using these commands; the choice remains until changed or the subformula ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '$$n+\scriptstyle n+\scriptscriptstyle n.$$' shows plus signs shrinking with style. Use \strut to adjust denominator height and \hfill to left/right flush numerators/denominators in fractions (useful for continued fractions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \strut and \hfill to refine fraction appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: \strut inserts invisible vertical space to make denominators taller; \hfill before numerator/denominator can produce flush-left or flush-right alignment instead of the default centering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: continued fractions using \displaystyle and \strut to force display-style denominators; \hfill stretches more than the glue TeX uses for centering, enabling flush alignment variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large operators and limit placement (\sum, \int; \limits, \nolimits, \displaylimits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols like \sum and \int are 'large operators'; TeX places limits above/below them in display style and as super/subscripts in text style by default. Use \limits, \nolimits, or \displaylimits to override.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: $$\sum x_n$$ (text style) vs $$\sum x_n$$ (display style). For integrals, limits are not set above/below even in display style by default; use \limits if you want that. \displaylimits restores normal conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-row limits using \atop with explicit script sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: To place two or more rows of limits under a large operator use \atop and enforce appropriate script sizing (e.g., \scriptstyle) so the lines are readable rather than tiny scriptscript size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: $$\sum_{\scriptstyle 0\le i\le m \atop \scriptstyle 0<j<n} P(i,j)$$. Without explicit size commands TeX may reduce the lines to scriptscript size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square root and delimiter extensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Square-root signs and many delimiters come in multiple sizes; the largest ones are extensible by repeating a vertical segment as needed. Delimiters may be constructed to any necessary height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nested roots show a variety of available glyphs; delimiters (parentheses, braces, brackets) similarly have repeatable extensions to reach required size for complex expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of delimiter sizing commands: \big, \Big, \biggl, \Biggl and directional variants
rubrics_metrics.description: To get delimiters slightly larger than ordinary use \bigl/\bigr; \Bigl/\Bigr are ~50% taller than \big and suited to displays; \biggl/\biggr and \Biggl/\Biggr are larger still (twice or ~2.5×).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \bigm/\Bigm/\biggm/\Biggm for middle (relation-like) delimiters (TeX will add spacing around them). Often \big and \bigg variants are used more than the largest ones. Examples show nesting readability improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimiters can act as ordinary, opening, closing, or middle symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Variants like \bigl/\bigr mark opening/closing delimiters; bare \big etc. produce ordinary symbol-like delimiters; \bigm produces a middle delimiter treated as a relation with spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example uses: \bigl(x-s(x)\bigr), \bigcup_n X_n \bigm\vert \bigcap_n Y_n. Choose the variant according to syntactic role to get correct spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic delimiter sizing with \left and \right
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \left( subformula \right) (and corresponding \left...\right...) to have TeX compute how tall delimiters need to be to enclose a subformula automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is usually preferable to manual \big/... sizing; it handles nested/complex subformulas correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never try to type literal braces; use control sequences for braces
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to specify a left brace or right brace simply by typing '{' or '}' since these are reserved for grouping; use \lbrace and \rbrace (or \{ and \}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grouping characters { } have special meaning and must not be used as literal delimiters; use the provided control sequences to get brace glyphs.
